summary: Round 3. NO CODE AND NO TESTS IN THIS DIFF -- nine files, two of them one-line javadoc pointers in src/main, the rest markdown and recorded verdicts -- so there is no production line to mutate and no test to weigh, and I say that rather than inventing a finding. Reviewed, as in rounds 1 and 2, as the falsifiability of the criteria M5.45f/g/h will be built and tested against. ALL THREE ROUND-2 MINORS ARE CLOSED WITH REAL WORDING AND NONE IS A RESTATEMENT OF THE DEFECT. (a) M5.45g criterion 5 now says ASSERTED, names the word it replaced, and names the surviving implementation (javadoc claims the offset does not advance while decodeInto catches, returns empty and advances) -- the documented-only discharge is gone. (b) M5.45h criteria 2 and 3 both say ASSERTED; criterion 2 carries the never-evicting Map<SegmentKey, byte[]> by name and cites SegmentCacheTest as the precedent that is asserted where it was not, and criterion 3 adds the 'fails every run' vs 'quietly empties every run' distinction, which is the whole content of the fix. (c) M5.45f criterion 3's artifact moved from the commit body into ADR-0043 itself; I confirmed the premise rather than taking it -- scripts/review.sh contains no git log, no COMMIT_EDITMSG and no --format=%B, so a list in the commit body is invisible to both roles at judgement time and sits outside the hash. NOTHING WAS WEAKENED: criterion 6's escape clause ('or it ships behind a flag that is OFF') is DELETED, which is strictly stronger than the round-2 form I passed, and M5.45h criterion 1's two round-1 fixes (ONE fetch AND ALL K RUNS DECODE THEIR OWN RECORDS, the fake counts INVOCATIONS not distinct urls) and M5.45g criterion 4's (bytes DECODED, the test fetcher serves only the ARRIVING url and throws otherwise) are present verbatim. No test file is staged, so testing.md rules 4-5 have no surface here. I also verified the round-1 majors I was asked to re-check: ADR-0043 no longer says 'M5.45c settles it' or 'M5.45c declines the range' anywhere -- every remaining M5.45c mention in the record and in the two src/main comments is explicitly historical ('it was M5.45c until that row was split'). FOUR MINORS, ALL THE SAME QUESTION THE TASK POSED: the new wording kills the implementation review named and leaves a NEIGHBOURING one open in each case. Each names a concrete implementation that satisfies the new wording and is still wrong, and each fix is one clause in the row that owns it. NONE BLOCKS, and under review.md rule 11 the right place for them is the taker's own review of f, g and h rather than a fourth round on 50 lines of prose -- I would rather they were recorded than fixed here.

findings.title: M5.45g criterion 5 now demands an assertion but still names neither the REQUIRED behaviour nor the LAYER, and ConsumerClient discards the delivery before decoding -- so a propagating throw loses the run one call later
findings.failure_scenario: The criterion reads 'A FETCH THAT FAILS HAS ASSERTED BEHAVIOUR' and names the forbidden outcome (swallow, empty batch, offset advances). It does not say what must hold instead, nor where it must be observed. TWO SURVIVING IMPLEMENTATIONS. (a) WRONG LAYER: a case at the seam only -- the test fetcher throws, the adapter rethrows, assertThrows green -- satisfies 'a fetch that fails has asserted behaviour' while ConsumerClient.decodeInto (client/src/main/java/binjava/client/ConsumerClient.java:76-93) gains a `catch (FetchFailed e) { return; }` beside its existing `catch (IOException e)`, which is the exact silent data loss the criterion exists to forbid. This is the M5.40a/M5.62 shape the row itself cites three times: the seam can behave and nothing asks the production path to. (b) RIGHT LAYER AND STILL WRONG: readNext polls the delivery OFF the queue at ConsumerClient.java:68 BEFORE calling decodeInto, so when the fetch throws and the exception propagates -- the behaviour the criterion's own example javadoc describes as correct ('propagates out of readNext, the offset does not advance') -- the delivery is ALREADY discarded. The next readNext serves the FOLLOWING delivery, whose firstOffset is past the failed run's records, so the consumer resumes beyond records nobody read. 'The offset does not advance' is true on the throwing call and the data is gone on the next one, with a case asserting the throw and every other criterion green. Under `direct` this is the normal case, not the corrupt-segment case: an expired grant and a 403 are both named in the criterion.
findings.suggestion: Name the behaviour and the layer: 'ASSERTED THROUGH ConsumerClient.readNext -- the failure is visible to the caller AND the same run is still readable afterwards, because readNext polls the delivery off the queue before decoding, so a propagating throw discards it and the next call resumes past records nobody read.'

findings.title: M5.45h criterion 2's 'NAMED AND ASSERTED' kills the never-evicting Map and leaves the UNBOUNDED-SIZE hold, which is the same C = 8 MiB vs C = 8 GiB defect the criterion says it closes
findings.failure_scenario: SURVIVING IMPLEMENTATION: the node-scoped owner holds exactly ONE segment, evicting the previous array on each new fetch. A case fetches segment A, lets its K runs decode, fetches B, and asserts A's bytes are released. Both halves the criterion names -- 'the ceiling and the eviction' -- are asserted, criterion 1's K = 64 single-segment case is untouched, criterion 3 is untouched. The bound is then ONE SEGMENT OF ARBITRARY SIZE, so the row's own sentence survives verbatim: 'M5's criterion 6 cannot tell C = 8 MiB from C = 8 GiB'. It is worse under `direct` than anywhere else in the tree, because a whole-object GET is bounded by nothing on the consumer side -- inline is capped by inlineCapBytes on the push channel and this path has no equivalent -- and the hold lives inside the OpenSearch node process. The precedent the criterion cites goes one step further than the criterion asks for: ingest/src/test/java/binjava/ingest/SegmentCacheTest.java:72 is aSegmentLARGERThanTheCeilingIsREFUSEDRatherThanAdmittedAndEvicted, a BYTE ceiling with a refusal, and the criterion asks only that a ceiling and an eviction be asserted.
findings.suggestion: Say what the bound is in and what happens at it: 'the bound is in BYTES and a segment larger than it is REFUSED rather than admitted and evicted, as SegmentCacheTest:72 pins it' -- otherwise an entry-count or one-slot bound satisfies the words.

findings.title: M5.45h criterion 3 now tells 'fails every run' from 'quietly empties every run' but says nothing about the failure's LIFETIME -- a memoized failed fetch satisfies it and stops the node ingesting for good
findings.failure_scenario: SURVIVING IMPLEMENTATION, and it is the natural one: 64 deliveries arrive at 64 independent readNext calls, so the obvious way to make them share one fetch is Map<SegmentKey, CompletableFuture<byte[]>> computeIfAbsent. Memoizing the FAILED future is the classic defect of that shape -- the failure must be removed from the map on completion, and nothing in criterion 3 asks for it. One 403 or one expired grant then fails all 64 runs VISIBLY, which is exactly what criterion 3 asserts and exactly what M5.40a's all-or-none rule wants, AND fails every later delivery for that segment forever, including ones carrying a fresh grant. Criterion 1's case uses a successful fetch and is green; criterion 2's bound is intact -- indeed the failed entry is small. The node stops ingesting that segment permanently after one recoverable error, with the failure loud each time, so an operator sees noise rather than the cause. The row's own framing invites this: 'unioning them needs a per-node HOLD of the segment or a barrier'.
findings.suggestion: Add the recovery half: 'and a LATER delivery for the same segment carrying a fresh grant succeeds -- a failed fetch is not cached, which is what a shared CompletableFuture does by default.'

findings.title: The 'no production fetcher until M5.45h' guard is a numbered criterion in M5.45g only; in M5.45f it is prose after the ACCEPTANCE list, so both rows can land green with the guard recorded nowhere
findings.failure_scenario: This is round 1's production major, one step removed. M5.45f's ACCEPTANCE is numbered (1) ADR answering both questions, (2) the amendment in ADR-0043, (3) the sweep artifact. The ordering obligation -- 'AND IF (a) PICKS A REAL ADAPTER, THE ADR SAYS IT IS NOT WIRED INTO A CONSUMER PATH UNTIL M5.45h' -- sits AFTER the list and is numbered nowhere, and the row explicitly delegates it: 'M5.45g's criterion 6 carries the obligation'. PATH TO THE BAD STATE: M5.45f lands with 1-3 green and no ordering sentence in the new ADR (the ADR is written to answer (a) and (b), and neither question is the ordering); M5.45g lands with criterion 6 green because nothing is wired, and the row closes -- a discharged criterion in a done row constrains nothing afterwards. The guard now exists in no open row and in no record, and any later row (a new 'ship the HTTP adapter' row, or M5.62's wiring) wires it before M5.45h. That is the round-1 state exactly, with the same invisibility: SPEC criterion 8 counts through the INGESTER's CountingBinStore and GrantIssuer's javadoc records that consumer-side GETs are invisible to it, so ~400 whole-object GETs per node per 8 MiB segment pass every gate. A guard whose only durable home is prose in a row that is not asked to assert it is the weaker of the two homes, which is the argument this very diff makes when it deletes criterion 6's escape clause.
findings.suggestion: Promote it: make it M5.45f criterion (4) -- 'if (a) picks a real adapter, the ADR states that it is NOT wired into a consumer path until M5.45h lands, and that sentence is in the record rather than in a row that will close'.

findings.title: M5.45f criterion 3's five grep patterns are an enumeration, and are exactly as complete as the enumeration (raised as the weakest of the five findings)
findings.failure_scenario: Naming byteStart, byteLen, M5.44, ADR-0043 and VERSION_3 makes the sweep re-runnable by a reviewer, which is the point and is a real improvement -- I ran it, and it returns 26 files. A site that argues the coordinates earn their place WITHOUT naming a field, a row id or the record is not in that set: ingest/src/main/java/binjava/ingest/FetchPolicyConfig.java:19 reads 'below it, shipping bytes across an AZ costs less than the GET it saves; above it, send coordinates' and the file contains none of the five patterns. It is a borderline site -- 'coordinates' there is the mode choice rather than byteStart/byteLen specifically -- which is why this is a nit and not a minor, but it is a concrete miss of the sweep as prescribed, and the cost of closing it is two more patterns.
findings.suggestion: Add `coordinates` and `byte range` to the pattern list, and say the artifact records the patterns actually run so the next reader can re-run the same sweep rather than a similar one.
